entry.title: A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean
entry.summary: A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean Delving Bitcoin · Nov 13, 2026The author shares a personal project on Delving Bitcoin that uses STARK proofs to verify parts of Bitcoin consensus. A 1.6 MB proof file is said to verify in a browser in about half a second, covering a header chain from genesis, a replay of blocks 935,001 to 972,500, and the UTXO set after block 972,500, whose hash matches Core's hash_serialized. Scripts and signatures are not covered, and the coin set relies on the same trust as assumeUTXO snapshots.

entry.title: Draft proposal for a post-quantum Bitcoin address format (bc1z) using ML-DSA-65 signatures
entry.summary: BIP Draft Post-Quantum Address Format (bc1z) using ML-DSA-65 Delving Bitcoin · Nov 13, 2026This forum post shares a draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposal for a new bc1z address format that uses ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204) post-quantum signatures. The address commits to a SHA-256 hash of the ML-DSA public key, which is revealed only in the witness at spend time, similar to P2WPKH. The author requests community feedback on address design, parameter choice, soft fork deployment, and migration paths for existing UTXOs.

entry.title: WARCoin: A Proposed 1:1 USD Stablecoin Using Serialized 7-Day Color Buckets and Burn-on-Egress Rules
entry.summary: [RFC] WARCoin: Deterministic 1:1 USD Stablecoin via Serialized 7-Day Color Ring Buffers and Burn-on-Egress Invariants ethresear.ch · Nov 13, 2026This request for comments proposes WARCoin, a deterministic 1:1 USD stablecoin designed to prevent infinite-mint bugs, cross-collateral contagion, and replay attacks. It accepts only USD deposits, burns serial numbers when funds leave, and organizes issuance into seven daily color buckets of 1,000 serials each. A global supply cap of 10^9 serials is enforced, with minting paused when limits are reached.

entry.title: More Meters or More Prices? Comparing One- and Multi-dimensional Ethereum Fee Mechanisms
entry.summary: More Meters or More Prices? One- vs. Multi-dimensional Fee Mechanisms on Ethereum ethresear.ch · Nov 13, 2026This Ethereum Research forum post compares one-dimensional fee mechanisms with the multidimensional fee market proposed in EIP-7999. The author raises the target-to-limit ratio of a normalized benchmark to 4/5 and replaces the EIP-1559 update rule with an EIP-4844-style update, measuring execution gas, state growth, and near-limit blocks. Higher ratios increase execution but push state growth away from its target and raise congestion. The EIP-4844-style update allows lower fees and more execution, but with more congestion.

entry.title: Multi-dimensional decentralization metrics and a double-spend rule open for critique
entry.summary: Multi-dimensional decentralization metrics, and an open question on first-broadcast double-spend rules ethresear.ch · Nov 12, 2026The author presents an open-source Apache-2.0 skill that lets LLM agents analyze blockchain architectures across several independent dimensions rather than a single number, and compares PoW, PoS, DAG, sharded designs and AOB. The post also describes AOB's first-broadcast-wins double-spend rule, which uses an estimated broadcast time t₀ to set waiting periods. The author asks the community to challenge the t₀ error tolerance, adversarial latency model, and eclipse threat model comparison.

entry.title: Seam: a trustless Zcash header checker on Base, plus private payment proofs
entry.summary: Seam: verifying Zcash headers on Base with EIP-152, and proving shielded payments without linking the chains ethresear.ch · Nov 12, 2026This forum post presents Seam, a contract on Base that verifies every Zcash block header against Zcash's consensus rules, including the Equihash solution, difficulty adjustment, time rules and cumulative work. Contracts can then read Zcash's best chain without relying on a bridge, committee or relayer. The post also describes building zero-knowledge proofs on top of this relay that show a shielded payment's amount and recipient without exposing transaction details to the EVM chain.

entry.title: Elastic Ethereum: an opinion post proposing protocol capacity that adjusts to measured resource pressure
entry.summary: Elastic Ethereum ethresear.ch · Nov 11, 2026This ethresear.ch opinion post outlines a possible design direction called Elastic Ethereum, rethinking scaling, availability, and finality through elasticity. It argues that Ethereum's block capacity is preconfigured, with no protocol-wide rule that adapts limits to measured resource pressure. Drawing on TCP congestion control as an example, the author proposes a closed feedback loop and uses mainnet propagation data to illustrate the cost of current safety margins.

entry.title: Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols: A Discussion Framework for Paying Miners Directly
entry.summary: Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion Delving Bitcoin · Nov 11, 2026This Delving Bitcoin post is a discussion framework on decentralized coinbase payout protocols (DCPPs) for mining pools, aiming to stimulate community research. It argues that paying each miner with a distinct coinbase output does not scale and describes the Rich List Attack, a form of payout settlement griefing. The authors review earlier designs, including Chris Belcher's payment hub, Braidpool's Rolling Coinbase Aggregation, and P2Poolv2's market-driven approach, noting that each is vulnerable to some form of griefing.

entry.title: Disclosure of a memory-exhaustion DoS vulnerability in Eclair 0.14.0
entry.summary: Disclosure: Memory-exhaustion DoS in Eclair 0.14.0 Delving Bitcoin · Nov 9, 2026This post discloses a memory-exhaustion denial-of-service flaw in Eclair 0.14.0, triggered via the start_batch message. Any peer able to connect to the node can make it buffer unlimited commitment_signed messages until memory runs out, without needing a channel. The cause is a missing lower-bound check on batch_size, which allows zero; the fix is in 0.14.1, and users are advised to upgrade.

entry.title: Solving PQC Bandwidth with Lattice HSMs: A Hardware Concept Discussion for Ethereum Validators
entry.summary: Solving PQC Bandwidth via Nybrind Wiesner Money & Lattice HSMs ethresear.ch · Nov 9, 2026The author proposes a conceptual hardware framework called LATTICE-NOTATION (LN) for post-quantum validation in decentralized networks such as Ethereum. It runs lattice computations inside a hardware security module and sends only compressed scalar proofs, aiming to ease bandwidth strain from large post-quantum keys and signatures like ML-KEM. The post also describes a quantum-state anti-cloning mechanism and invites community critique.

entry.title: Should wallets default to Taproot or SegWit receive addresses while some services reject bc1p?
entry.summary: Should wallets default to Taproot or SegWit receive addresses while some services still reject bc1p? Delving Bitcoin · Nov 8, 2026A business development and support staff member at Gem Wallet posted on Delving Bitcoin about users receiving "invalid address" errors when withdrawing to exchanges or other services. The Taproot (bc1p) addresses are valid, but some services do not accept them. The post asks wallet teams whether they default to Taproot or SegWit receive addresses, how they offer a choice, and how to tell which services accept bc1p.

entry.title: Folding vs full-verifier recursion for post-quantum signature aggregation in leanVM: measurements and negative results
entry.summary: Folding vs full-verifier recursion for PQ signature aggregation in leanVM: measurements and negative results ethresear.ch · Nov 8, 2026The author measured hash-based accumulation schemes such as WARP against leanVM's full-verifier recursion for aggregating post-quantum signatures on an 8 GB M2 laptop. Inside a single aggregator, the accumulation designs did not outperform leanVM's recursion. Folding signature verifications directly cost far more per signature than leanVM's existing approach.

entry.title: GKR protocol with a machine-checked core and a faster sparse prover with identical proofs
entry.summary: GKR with a Machine-Checked Core, and a Sparse Prover Made Faster with Byte-Identical Proofs ethresear.ch · Nov 8, 2026This post describes StateSync-GKR, which gives the first machine-checked soundness bound for GKR on general layered circuits, in Isabelle/HOL. The bound is applied to a soundness proof for sparse-Merkle updates. Release 1.2 of the sparse prover proves 2.41 to 2.71 times faster and produces byte-identical proofs.

entry.title: How large can EIP-8141's validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark
entry.summary: How large can EIP-8141's validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark ethresear.ch · Nov 7, 2026A technical discussion on the Ethereum Research forum by the Nethermind team. It notes that EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation gas at 100k, which is too low for privacy transfers and post-quantum signatures. The authors simulate a denial-of-service attack on a Nethermind node, flooding it with transactions that use the full validation budget and then fail, at caps from 100k to 500k. They report that with an in-client protection that pauses transaction validation during block processing, a cap of 300k is viable.

entry.title: A privacy pool on frame transactions: which parts work and which do not yet
entry.summary: A privacy pool on frame transactions: what works, and the case that does not yet ethresear.ch · Nov 6, 2026Nethermind researchers built a privacy pool using BN254 Groth16 proofs on frame transactions, where the pool itself pays gas so private withdrawals need no relayer. They report a withdrawal costs 679,322 gas on a test node. Two problems remain open: the proof check exceeds the EIP-8141 validation gas cap, and a pool cannot pay for calls made from the user's own address.

entry.title: TULIP: A permissionless decentralized identity concept
entry.summary: TULIP: Permissionless Decentralized Identity Delving Bitcoin · Nov 6, 2026The author proposes a pseudonymous identity system that avoids central coordinators and uses the Bitcoin blockchain as the timestamping and ordering authority for identity key changes. Keys rotate through a precommitted Taproot chain, keeping the onchain footprint small. A linked whitepaper, Tuliproot, also suggests a 4-byte witness header to help index important state-change transactions.

entry.title: Walraswap: an equilibrium-based decentralized exchange that integrates external AMM liquidity
entry.summary: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity ethresear.ch · Nov 6, 2026This paper presents Walraswap, a decentralized exchange design based on equilibrium theory for exchange economies, which settles batches of trade orders together and can incorporate external AMM liquidity. The authors argue that equilibrium requires uniform clearing prices and inclusion of all available orders, and they propose governance by a DAO that elects solvers, with public order flow to discourage censorship. The paper also presents theoretical results on the existence, uniqueness of net trades, and computation via convex optimization.

entry.title: Question about direct messaging on the forum

They have added the artist's song "Off the Chain" to btcplaylist.com and want listeners to be able to zap the artist. Unable to find a direct message option on the forum, they raised the question in this thread.

entry.title: Full OP_RETURN value pruning for satd Bitcoin nodes
entry.summary: Full OP_RETURN value pruning Delving Bitcoin · Nov 3, 2026The satd Bitcoin node implementation adds an optional feature to prune OP_RETURN output values from on-disk block files using hole-punching. It is controlled by options such as -pruneopreturn, -pruneopreturnsize and -restoreopreturns. The author argues this lets operators express preferences without breaking consensus, but notes disk usage may increase rather than decrease and that pruned nodes cannot serve some block data.

entry.title: Storage-optimized replay protection: packed flag lanes versus per-flag booleans, and whether the protocol could offer cheaper storage.
entry.summary: Storage-optimized replay protection: from hash => bool to packed flag lanes, and can the protocol offer better? ethresear.ch · Nov 3, 2026The post covers protocols that must permanently record one small flag per event, such as privacy-pool nullifiers and unordered nonces. It compares three layouts: one boolean per flag, a 256-flag bitmap word, and per-party lanes within a word, with gas estimates for each. The author argues that packing can only approach fixed cost floors, and asks whether the execution layer could offer replay flags directly at a price suited to that use.
